title: Confidentiality, data protection and information sharing
blurb: Protect confidential information, share it when care or safety requires, and apply the Caldicott and UK GDPR principles.
question: Thomas, 35, is an inpatient. He tells the nurse he intends to stab his ex-partner, names her and says he knows where she lives. He asks the nurse to keep this to herself. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: A duty to protect and a duty to share
teach.body: As a nurse you owe a duty of confidentiality to everyone in your care: information about them is shared appropriately and they are told how it is used (Code 5). But confidentiality is not absolute. Caldicott principle 7 states that the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect confidentiality, and Code 5.4 allows sharing when patient safety and public protection override confidentiality. In plain English: guard it carefully, share it purposefully.

teach.body: Thomas has made a specific threat of serious violence against a named person. The nurse tells him honestly that she cannot keep this confidential, informs the nurse in charge and medical team at once, and follows local policy for disclosure to protect his ex-partner. Code 5.4 and 17.2 support sharing when safety overrides confidentiality, and statutory guidance accepts an overriding public interest where others are at risk of serious harm. She records what was said, to whom it was shared and why.

teach.h: Children: the s16LA duty to share
teach.body: Since 30 September 2026, s16LA of the Children Act 2004 requires bodies under the s11 duty (including NHS bodies) to share information they consider relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare with other such bodies where it may help their safeguarding functions, unless disclosure would be more harmful to the child than not disclosing. There is no threshold, consent is not required, and such a disclosure does not breach any obligation of confidence.
teach.cite: Children Act 2004 s16LA (Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026)

teach.caption: Code 5.3: confidentiality continues after death. Code 10.5: keep records secure.

teach.text: Having system access is not the same as having a reason. Caldicott 4 means you look only at records you need for your role. And 'next of kin' has no automatic right to information about an adult with capacity: share with family as far as the law allows and in line with the person's wishes (Code 5.5).

items: Code 5: privacy, informing people, confidentiality after death, sharing when safety overrides.
Caldicott: justify, necessary, minimum, need-to-know, responsibilities, law, duty to share, inform.
UK GDPR: lawful, purpose, minimisation, accuracy, storage, security, accountability.
Share without consent when required by law or when a serious risk to others outweighs confidentiality; record it.
Children: s16LA duty to share safeguarding information, in force 30 September 2026.

summary: You can now apply Code 5, the eight Caldicott principles and the UK GDPR principles to everyday decisions, recognise when sharing without consent is justified by law or public interest, and use the new s16LA duty for children.

A.q: Mr Evans, 77, is going home with a leg ulcer needing daily dressings from district nurses. The ward nurse hesitates to send details without his written consent. Which Caldicott principle supports sharing?
options: Use the minimum necessary personal confidential data
Inform patients and service users how their data is being used
Access should be on a strict need-to-know basis for every user
Sharing for individual care matters as much as protecting it
A.why: Caldicott principle 7: the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect confidentiality. Sharing with the district nurses supports his direct care.

whyNot.0: Principle 3 governs how much to share, not whether sharing for care is supported.
whyNot.1: Principle 8 is about transparency, not the case for sharing.
whyNot.2: Principle 4 limits who accesses data; it does not support sharing.

A.q: Mr Carter died on the ward last week. A local journalist phones, saying she is writing a tribute, and asks what illness he died from. What should the nurse do?
options: Share the cause, as confidentiality ends with death
Share it if his widow agrees on the telephone
Give general details without naming the condition
Decline, as confidentiality continues after death
A.why: Code 5.3: respect that a person's right to privacy and confidentiality continues after they have died. There is no lawful basis to disclose to a journalist.

whyNot.0: Confidentiality does not end at death.
whyNot.1: Telephone agreement from someone unverified does not justify disclosure to the press.
whyNot.2: Any health details given to a journalist breach his confidentiality.

A.q: Femi, a nurse, sees that her neighbour has been admitted to another ward in the trust. She can access the electronic record. What is the correct view?
options: Viewing it is acceptable if she does not share the details
Viewing it breaches the need-to-know principle
Viewing it is acceptable if the neighbour would not mind
Viewing it is acceptable if she is checking on welfare
A.why: Caldicott principle 4: access on a strict need-to-know basis. System access does not create a right to view records of people not in her care (Code 5.1).

whyNot.0: Accessing the record is itself the breach, whether or not she shares it.
whyNot.2: Assumed approval is not consent and does not create a care need.
whyNot.3: Personal concern is not a professional need to know.

B.q: Thomas, 35, tells the nurse he intends to stab his ex-partner, names her and says he knows where she lives. He asks the nurse to keep it confidential. What should she do?
options: Keep his confidence, as he told her in a therapeutic role
Ask him to promise not to act, then record the discussion
Tell him this cannot stay confidential and escalate it now
Wait to see whether he repeats the threat before sharing it
B.why: Code 5.4: share when patient safety and public protection override confidentiality; Code 17.2: share if someone may be at risk of harm. A specific threat to a named person justifies disclosure in the public interest.

whyNot.0: A therapeutic relationship does not outweigh a serious risk to an identifiable person.
whyNot.1: A promise does not remove the risk; the threat needs escalation.
whyNot.3: Delay leaves the named person at risk.

B.q: A caller says she is Mrs Green's daughter and asks how her mother's operation went. Mrs Green, 70, has capacity. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give a brief update, as the caller is close family
Transfer the call to the surgeon who operated
Decline to discuss it and ask the caller to visit in person
Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts first
B.why: Code 5.1-5.2 and 5.5: share with family as far as the law allows, in line with the person's wishes. The nurse checks whether Mrs Green agrees to information being given to this caller.

whyNot.0: The caller's identity is unverified and Mrs Green's wishes are unknown.
whyNot.1: The surgeon would face the same question; the patient's wishes come first.
whyNot.2: Refusing all contact may be unnecessary if Mrs Green is happy for her daughter to be told.

B.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has been breached?
options: Integrity and confidentiality (security)
Purpose limitation of the data collected
Accuracy of the data being processed
Storage limitation of personal records
B.why: UK GDPR Article 5 requires appropriate security against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5: keep records secure.

whyNot.1: The sheet was produced for care; the problem is how it was secured.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the data is inaccurate.
whyNot.3: Storage limitation concerns keeping data longer than needed, not leaving it unsecured.

C.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She asks staff not to tell anyone. Under the law from 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
options: Respect her wishes, as she is an adult with capacity
Ask Kerry's consent again once she is less distressed
Share the relevant information with children's services
Record it and pass it to the GP in the discharge letter
C.why: Children Act 2004 s16LA requires NHS bodies to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, with no threshold and without needing consent; the disclosure does not breach confidence. A young child alone needs an immediate response.

whyNot.0: Her capacity does not override the duty to share information to safeguard her son.
whyNot.1: Consent is not required, and waiting leaves the child at risk.
whyNot.3: A discharge letter is far too slow for a child alone at home now.

C.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a home care agency. The patient has capacity and has refused. Whose advice should the nurse in charge seek?
options: The trust's Caldicott Guardian
The patient's next of kin
The care agency's own registered manager
The Information Commissioner
C.why: The Caldicott Guardian protects confidentiality and enables appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions, and statutory guidance advises involving them in public interest decisions (Care and support statutory guidance 14.188).

whyNot.1: Relatives cannot decide about an adult's confidential information.
whyNot.2: The agency is the potential recipient, not an independent adviser.
whyNot.3: The ICO regulates data protection; it does not make individual clinical sharing decisions.

C.q: Ruth is referring Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery, to a dietitian. The record also contains past psychiatric history and details of a divorce. What should she include?
options: The whole record so the dietitian has full context
The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything in the record except the psychiatric history
A summary agreed with Mrs Smith's husband
C.why: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary data; UK GDPR data minimisation: adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.

whyNot.0: Sending the whole record shares far more than is needed.
whyNot.2: Removing one item still sends irrelevant personal details such as the divorce.
whyNot.3: Her husband has no role in deciding what is shared about an adult with capacity.

reteach.title: Ask: who, why, how much, and on what basis?
reteach.question: If you had to decide in 30 seconds whether to share something, what would you ask yourself?

blocks.body: WHO is asking, and do they need it for this person's care or safety? WHY: is there a clear purpose? HOW MUCH: what is the minimum that achieves it? On what BASIS: direct care, consent, a legal duty, or a serious risk to others that outweighs confidentiality? If you can answer all four, share and record. If you can't, ask the nurse in charge or Caldicott Guardian.

letters.word: Basis: care, consent, law, public interest

explain.body: Respect privacy (5.1), tell people how information is used (5.2), confidentiality continues after death (5.3), share when safety and public protection override (5.4), share with people and families what they want or need, as far as the law allows (5.5).

test.q: Which Code clause supports sharing information without consent when someone is at serious risk?
options: Clause 5.4
Clause 5.3
Clause 5.1
Clause 5.2
test.why: Code 5.4: share necessary information when the interests of patient safety and public protection override the need for confidentiality.

whyNot.3: 5.2 concerns informing people how information is used.

explain.body: Eight principles: justify the purpose; use only when necessary; minimum necessary; need-to-know access; everyone understands responsibilities; comply with the law; the duty to share for care is as important as the duty to protect; inform patients.

test.q: A nurse sends only the wound details, not the full history, to the tissue viability nurse. Which principle is she applying?
options: Inform patients how data is used
Comply with the law
Use the minimum necessary data
Justify the purpose for using it
test.why: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data.

whyNot.0: Principle 8 is about transparency with patients.
whyNot.1: Principle 6 is about legal compliance generally.
whyNot.3: Principle 1 is about having a purpose, not limiting the amount.

explain.body: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality (security); accountability.

test.q: A patient's allergy is recorded against the wrong drug and not corrected. Which UK GDPR principle is breached?
options: Storage limitation
Accuracy
Purpose limitation
Accountability
test.why: UK GDPR requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date.

whyNot.0: Storage limitation is about how long data is kept.
whyNot.2: Purpose limitation is about using data for its stated purpose.
whyNot.3: Accountability is about demonstrating compliance overall.

explain.body: Justified when required by law (for example FGM in under-18s, notifiable diseases, s16LA for children) or when a serious risk to others outweighs confidentiality (public interest). Share the minimum, tell the person if safe, and record.

test.q: When a nurse shares information in the public interest without consent, what else should she do?
options: Share the full record to avoid omissions
Tell the person's family what was shared
Ask the person to sign a retrospective consent
Record what was shared, with whom and why
test.why: Decisions to share without consent must be justified and recorded so they can be reviewed (Code 10.2, 10.4; Caldicott 1 and 3).

whyNot.0: The minimum necessary should be shared (Caldicott 3).
whyNot.1: Telling family would be a further disclosure without a basis.
whyNot.2: Retrospective consent is not a requirement and may not be appropriate.
